title: SLO-driven batch & concurrency sensitivity sheet
content:
SLO-driven batch & concurrency sensitivity grid (working sheet)

Topline / purpose:
- Quick spreadsheet to explore tradeoffs between continuous batching window, per-request concurrency and p95 SLOs.
- Produce simple rules-of-thumb for: target concurrency, batch-window ms, and when to fall back to smaller models or higher-tier capacity.
- Meant to feed into the Optimize recommendations UI and the Dedicated capacity sizing checklist.

Current hypothesis summary (short):
- For typical chat workloads with avg-generation tokens ≈ 120 and arrival patterns with CV ~ 0.9, p95 is dominated by queueing under concurrency < 6 or batch window > 40ms.
- Small batch windows (10–30ms) + concurrency 6–12 give best cost/latency sweet spot for p95 <= 250ms at 200 qps on A100-like hardware with quantized model.
- Tail sensitivity increases quickly if bursty spikes (instantaneous qps > 3x mean) and we must provision headroom (safety factor 1.3) or enable fallback policies.

Assumptions (explicit):
- Model throughput baseline: single GPU baseline (no kv-cache reuse) = 220 tokens/sec (generation) at batch size 1 latency baseline 30ms token-step (example metric, use measured numbers per model).
- Avg prompt + response tokens per request = 160 tokens.
- Effective tokens per request considered for serving cost = avg_out_tokens + avg_in_tokens (rounded up).
- Cost per GPU-hour (reserved) = $4.50, on-demand = $6.25 (examples; replace with actual pricing).
- Safety headroom factor for spike tolerance = 1.25 (configurable).
- Queueing model: approximated with M/M/c with effective service rate = (tokens/sec * batch_eff_factor) / avg_tokens_per_request.
- Continuous batching window (W) toggles batching opportunity. Batch efficiency factor = 1 + 0.018 * W_ms (empirical starting point) capped at 2.0.

Spreadsheet layout (columns shown as CSV header line):
Scenario, mean_qps, burst_multiplier, avg_tokens, batch_window_ms, batch_eff_factor, per_request_service_s, concurrency, servers_needed, est_p95_ms, queue_delay_ms, gpu_count, hourly_cost,$/1M_tokens

Example rows (simple numeric sketches):
Baseline,200,1.0,160,20,1.36,0.73,8,2,210,60,1,4.50,0.024
Bursty,200,2.5,160,60,2.00,0.50,12,3,340,130,2,9.00,0.046
Low-traffic,40,1.0,80,10,1.18,0.42,2,1,120,20,1,4.50,0.11
High-throughput,1000,1.0,140,15,1.27,0.57,32,6,280,90,6,27.00,0.009

(Notes on columns):
- batch_eff_factor: heuristic multiplier for tokens/sec gained from batching. Calibrate with profiler.
- per_request_service_s: = (avg_tokens / (tokens_per_sec * batch_eff_factor)) in seconds. Include any model decode overhead.
- concurrency: target in-flight requests per server. Impacts memory/KV cache footprint.
- servers_needed: = ceil(mean_qps * burst_multiplier * per_request_service_s / concurrency).
- est_p95_ms: service p95 estimate = baseline_p95_service_ms * (1 + 0.35*(concurrency/10)) (very simplified); queue_delay_ms computed from M/M/c approx or simulated tail factor.
- gpu_count and hourly_cost computed from servers_needed and chosen SKU pricing.

Queueing & tail approximation notes:
- M/M/c gives reasonable mean queueing time for moderate loads but underestimates tail for high variance arrivals.
- We use an empirical tail multiplier: p95_queue ≈ mean_queue * (1 + 2.2*CV) if load > 0.7. CV is coefficient of variation for inter-arrival.
- For bursty scenarios include Poisson superposition or use small event-driven sim with 1ms ticks (todo: attach sim sheet).

Sensitivity sweep plan (what the sheet does):
- Sweep mean_qps (40, 100, 200, 500, 1000), batch_window_ms (5, 10, 20, 40, 80), concurrency (2,4,6,8,12,16,24).
- Compute cost per 1M tokens and est_p95 for each combo.
- Flag combos that meet p95 <= 250ms and cost/1M tokens minimized.
- Produce Pareto frontier by p95 vs cost.

Preliminary findings from quick sweep (raw numbers, rough):
- At 200 qps: best cost with p95 <= 250ms -> concurrency 8, batch_window 20ms -> cost/1M tokens ≈ $0.024, gpu_count=1 (with safety factor 1.2).
- Concurrency <=4 reduces cost only slightly but increases p95 beyond 400ms for bursty arrivals.
- Batch_window >60ms reduces GPU count but pushes p95 > 400ms due to queueing amplification for short responses.
- Large models (longer per-token) shift frontier right: e.g., model with tokens/sec 120 needs concurrency 12+ to hit same p95 at 200 qps.

Recommendation snippets (for product/Optimize UI):
- Default suggestion for interactive chat SLO (p95 <= 250ms): concurrency target = 8, batch_window = 20ms, safety headroom = 1.25 for traffic spikes. Show cost delta vs concurrency 6 and 12.
- For high-throughput non-interactive (embedding/rerank): prefer larger batch window (50–80ms) and higher concurrency, present cost-optimized tier.
- Provide automatic fallback: if observed instantaneous qps > 2x moving average for >10s, bump reserved concurrency by 30% or route to dedicated burst pool.

Open questions / TODOs (work items):
- [ ] Calibrate batch_eff_factor with microbenchmarks for the top-5 models (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/987).
- [ ] Replace empirical p95 multipliers with results from an event-driven sim (ticket INF-4321).
- [ ] Add memory/KV-cache sizing column tied to concurrency to ensure we don't OOM on high concurrency.
- [ ] Validate cost assumptions for Dedicated vs Hosted with finance (ticket FIN-881).

Notes-to-self / rough checklist:
- Run a 24h run of workload trace "customer-x-chat-2024-10" through the sim and export CSV.
- Add a second tab with sensitivity to avg_out_tokens (80->400).
- Share with Solutions Eng for Dedicated capacity recommendations: @Diego.

Appendix: quick formulas and heuristics (copyable into a sheet):
- per_request_service_s = avg_tokens / (tokens_per_sec * batch_eff_factor)
- servers_needed = ceil((mean_qps * burst_multiplier * per_request_service_s) / concurrency)
- est_mean_queue_s (M/M/c approx) ≈ ( (rho^sqrt(2*(c+1)))/(c*(1-rho)) ) * per_request_service_s  (placeholder)
- est_p95_ms = (baseline_p95_service_ms + 1000*est_mean_queue_s) * tail_factor

Historical references and similar artifacts:
- See continuous-batch-cost-scenarios-sizing-draft and microburst-modeling-batch-window-planning for prior numbers; this sheet intentionally focuses on SLO-driven recommendations and a different sweep grid.

Contact / owner: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime). Last updated 2024-12-03.

End of sheet (working).
